subject: Culture
title: Ley Lines and Geomancy
description: One-minute skill: Ley Lines and Geomancy.

hook.text: In 1921 Alfred Watkins noticed that ancient British sites fell on straight lines across the landscape.

buildup.text: He called them 'ley lines' and proposed they were ancient trading routes connecting sacred landmarks.

discovery.text: Chinese feng shui operates similarly—mapping invisible energy flows to determine where to build temples and tombs.

twist.text: Statisticians showed that random points on any map form apparent alignments. Ley lines may be pattern-seeking.

climax.text: Yet cultures worldwide independently decided some spots concentrate spiritual energy. The pattern is universal.

punchline.text: Whether real or imagined, sacred maps shape real cities.

details.summary: Ley lines are the theory that ancient sacred sites align in straight lines across landscapes, suggesting an intentional energy grid. While mainstream archaeology rejects ley lines as coincidence, the concept has inspired geomancy — the practice of reading spiritual energy in the landscape — for.
details.whyItMatters: Ley lines reveal the human desire to find hidden order in the world. Whether real energy or pattern-seeking illusion, the concept shapes how millions understand the relationship between land and spirit.
takeaways: Alfred Watkins proposed ley lines in 1921 after noticing site alignments
Mainstream archaeology considers ley line alignments coincidental
The concept inspired New Age beliefs about Earth energy grids

faq.question: What are ley lines exactly?
faq.answer: In 1921, Alfred Watkins noticed that ancient churches, standing stones, and hillforts in Britain seemed to align in straight lines across the landscape. He proposed these 'ley lines' marked ancient trackways.

faq.question: Is there any evidence for ley lines?
faq.answer: Statistically, no. With thousands of ancient sites scattered across any landscape, straight-line alignments are mathematically inevitable by chance. Computer simulations show that randomly distributed points produce just as many alignments as actual sacred sites.
